meta: 162 predict-the-output questions, Lydia Hallie style: read the snippet, predict the output out loud, then open the answer.
Every output here was produced by actually running the code on CPython 3.11.15.
Answers are closed by default (collapsible Obsidian callouts; on GitHub they render open).

The 140 🔴 High, 🟡 Medium and Trap questions also have a Go deeper toggle inside the answer, closed by default too. Each one follows the same shape: Under the hood (what CPython actually does, with a small picture where it helps) → Why the obvious guess fails (traps) or The edge cases → Try a variant (one more snippet, run on 3.11.15) → In real code.
The 96 in the file name is this file's item number in py_index_v4.md, not a question count.

Names, Objects & Core Types (Q1–Q12)

1. What's the output? 🔴 High · 🪤 Trap

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)
print(a)
Answer

Output

[1, 2, 3, 4]

Assignment never copies. b = a binds a second name to the same list object. Mutating through b is visible through a. Python variables are labels on objects, not boxes holding values.

Go deeper

Under the hood. A Python variable is a name stored in a namespace (a dict for module globals, a fast-locals array inside a function), and every name holds a reference to an object on the heap. b = a copies the reference, not the list. Both names now point at one PyListObject, whose reference count went from 1 to 2.

a ──┐
    ├──▶ [1, 2, 3, 4]   one list object, refcount 2
b ──┘

Why the obvious guess fails. People coming from C, Java primitives or spreadsheets picture b = a as "make b equal to a", meaning a copy. Python never copies on assignment, argument passing or return. A copy happens only when you ask for one: a[:], list(a), a.copy() or copy.deepcopy(a).

Try a variant. id() shows the identity directly:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
c = a.copy()
print(id(a) == id(b), id(a) == id(c))

True False

In real code. This is why a function that "fills in" a list you passed it changes the caller's list, and why storing a config dict on two objects can link them by accident. In an interview, say it in one sentence: "Names are labels bound to objects; assignment rebinds a label, it never copies the object."

2. What's the output? 🔴 High · 🪤 Trap

a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)
x = int("257")
y = int("257")
print(x is y, x == y)
Answer

Output

True
False True

CPython pre-allocates and caches small ints from -5 to 256, so every 256 is the same object. 257 built at runtime gets a fresh object each time, so is (identity) is False while == (value) is True. Rule: use == for values and is only for singletons like None.

Go deeper

Under the hood. CPython keeps a pre-built array of small int objects for -5 to 256 (_PyLong_SMALL_INTS), and every operation that produces one of those values returns the cached object. int("257") is computed at runtime and is above the range, so each call allocates a new PyLongObject. is compares addresses, == calls int.__eq__ and compares values.

Expression Small-int cache? is
256 and 256 yes, same cached object True
int("257") twice no, two allocations False
257 twice as literals in one code block compiler may share one constant can be True

Why the obvious guess fails. The last row is why people "see" 257 is 257 print True in a script and conclude the cache is bigger. The compiler deduplicates equal constants inside one code object. That's a compile-time accident, not a guarantee, and it disappears as soon as the value comes from input, arithmetic or another module.

Try a variant. Arithmetic results go through the cache only when they land in range:

x = 200
print((x + 56) is 256, (x + 57) is 257)

True False

In real code. Linters flag x is 5 (SyntaxWarning: "is" with a literal since 3.8) because it works for small values in testing and breaks on real data. Keep is for singletons: None, True, False, Ellipsis and sentinel objects you create with object().

3. What's the output? 🟡 Medium · 🪤 Trap

print(type(True), True + True, isinstance(True, int))
Answer

Output

<class 'bool'> 2 True

bool is a subclass of int: True == 1 and False == 0. That's why True + True == 2 and sum(flags) counts the Trues in a list.

Go deeper

Under the hood. class bool(int) is literally how it's defined in C: PyBool_Type sets tp_base = &PyLong_Type, and True/False are two pre-built int objects with values 1 and 0. Arithmetic is inherited from int, so True + True runs int.__add__ and returns a plain int (2), not a bool.

Why the obvious guess fails. You'd expect a type error or True back, because in most languages booleans aren't numbers. In Python the subclass relationship means a bool is accepted anywhere an int is, including as a list index (["no", "yes"][True] is "yes") and as a dict key that collides with 1.

Try a variant. Counting and the dict collision:

flags = [True, False, True, True]
print(sum(flags), {1: "one", True: "yes"}, type(True + 0).__name__)

3 {1: 'yes'} int

In real code. The subclass relation bites in validation: isinstance(True, int) is True, so a check like "is this a positive int?" accepts True. JSON schemas, Pydantic models and argument checks that must reject booleans test type(x) is int or check for bool first.

4. What's the output? 🔴 High · 🪤 Trap

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9)
Answer

Output

False
0.30000000000000004
True

Floats are IEEE-754 binary, and 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so the rounding errors add up. Compare with a tolerance (math.isclose), or use decimal.Decimal for money.

Go deeper

Under the hood. A float is an IEEE-754 binary64 number: 52 bits of fraction, so it stores the nearest binary fraction to what you typed. 0.1 is really 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827…, and 0.2 and 0.3 are rounded too. The sum of two rounded values lands on a different neighbouring float than the rounded 0.3, one ULP (unit in the last place) away.

0.1 + 0.2  → 0.30000000000000004440892098500626…
0.3        → 0.29999999999999998889776975374843…
              these are adjacent floats, not the same one

Why the obvious guess fails. print(0.1) shows 0.1, so it looks exact. Since Python 3.1, repr prints the shortest string that round-trips to the same float, which hides the error until arithmetic exposes it. The comparison is exact bit equality, so a one-ULP difference makes it False.

Try a variant. Decimal built from strings and math.isclose both give the human answer:

from decimal import Decimal
import math
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3), Decimal(0.1))

True
True 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

In real code. Money goes in Decimal (built from strings, never from floats) or in integer cents. Tests compare floats with pytest.approx or math.isclose (default relative tolerance 1e-09). Never use a float as a dict key or in a == check after arithmetic.

5. What's the output? 🟡 Medium · 🪤 Trap

print(7 // 2, -7 // 2, 7 % -3, -7 % 3)
Answer

Output

3 -4 -2 2

// is floor division and rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero, so -7 // 2 == -4. % takes the sign of the divisor, which keeps a == (a // b) * b + a % b true. C and Java truncate toward zero instead, so this catches people coming from those languages.

Go deeper

Under the hood. Python defines // as floor division, rounding toward −∞, and then defines % so that the identity a == (a // b) * b + a % b always holds. That forces the remainder to take the sign of the divisor. C, Java and Go truncate toward zero, so their % takes the sign of the dividend.

Expression Python (floor) C / Java (truncate)
-7 // 2 -4 -3
-7 % 3 2 -1
7 % -3 -2 1

Why the obvious guess fails. Most people learned division as "chop the decimals", which is truncation. That matches floor division only for positive operands, so the surprise appears only with negatives, often in date or index arithmetic where negatives show up rarely.

Try a variant. divmod returns both parts, and math.fmod gives you C-style truncation:

import math
print(divmod(-7, 2), math.fmod(-7, 3), int(-7 / 2))

(-4, 1) -1.0 -3

In real code. Python's choice makes i % n always land in 0..n-1 for positive n, which is exactly what you want for circular buffers, hashing into buckets and "day of week" arithmetic. Porting code from C or Java? Check every % and // that can see a negative number.

6. What's the output? 🟡 Medium

print(bool([]), bool([0]), bool(""), bool(" "), bool(0.0), bool(None))
Answer

Output

False True False True False False

Falsy values: None, False, zero of any numeric type, and empty containers or strings. Everything else is truthy. [0] is a non-empty list, so it's truthy. " " has one character, so it's truthy too.

Go deeper

Under the hood. bool(x) asks the object: CPython calls __bool__ if the type defines it, otherwise __len__ (non-zero length means true), and if neither exists the object is truthy. Built-in containers implement __len__, numbers implement __bool__ (zero is false), and None is hard-wired to false.

bool(x):  has __bool__? ─yes─▶ use it
              │no
          has __len__?  ─yes─▶ len(x) != 0
              │no
          True

The edge cases. Truthiness looks at emptiness, not contents. [0], [None], [[]] and " " are all truthy because they have one element. 0.0, 0j, Decimal(0) and Fraction(0) are falsy because they're zero. A class you write is truthy by default, even with every attribute empty, until you define __bool__ or __len__.

Try a variant. A user class decides its own truthiness:

class Basket:
    def __init__(self, items): self.items = items
    def __len__(self): return len(self.items)
print(bool(Basket([])), bool(Basket([0])), bool(object()))

False True True

In real code. if items: is the idiomatic emptiness check, but it treats 0, "" and None the same. When 0 is a valid value (a price, a count, a port), write if x is not None:. NumPy arrays and pandas Series refuse bool() with more than one element and raise ValueError: truth value ... is ambiguous.

7. What's the output? 🟡 Medium · 🪤 Trap

print(1 < 2 < 3)
print(3 > 2 > 1 == 1)
print((3 > 2) > 1)
Answer

Output

True
True
False

Comparisons chain: a < b < c means a < b and b < c, and b is evaluated once. 3 > 2 > 1 == 1 becomes 3>2 and 2>1 and 1==1, which is True. Parentheses break the chain: (3 > 2) is True, and True > 1 is 1 > 1, which is False.

Go deeper

Under the hood. The compiler turns a op1 b op2 c into a op1 b and b op2 c, evaluating b once and short-circuiting. In bytecode you can see a COPY/SWAP of the middle value and a conditional jump after each comparison. Every comparison operator chains this way: <, >, ==, !=, <=, >=, is, is not, in, not in.

3 > 2 > 1 == 1   →   (3 > 2) and (2 > 1) and (1 == 1)   →   True
(3 > 2) > 1      →   True > 1   →   1 > 1               →   False

Why the obvious guess fails. In C and JavaScript 3 > 2 > 1 is evaluated left to right as (3 > 2) > 1, which is true > 1, which is false. Python readers who know those languages either expect that, or assume Python does the same thing for ==. The parentheses force the C reading, which is why line three differs.

Try a variant. The middle operand really runs once:

def mid():
    print("mid called")
    return 5
print(1 < mid() < 10)

mid called
True

In real code. Range checks read naturally: 0 <= i < len(xs). The danger is chaining with in or is by accident, for example x == y in z (see #156), which reads like a single test but is two. When in doubt, add parentheses.

8. What's the output? 🟢 Low

print(None == False, None is None, not None)
Answer

Output

False True True

None is falsy but not equal to False. It's the only instance of NoneType, so the idiom is x is None. not None is True because of truthiness.

9. What's the output? 🟡 Medium · 🪤 Trap

x = 10
def f():
    print(x)
x = 20
f()
Answer

Output

20

A function looks up global names when it runs, not when it's defined. By the time f() is called, x has been rebound to 20.

Go deeper

Under the hood. A function body compiles x to LOAD_GLOBAL x because f never assigns to it. That instruction looks the name up in the module's __dict__ every time the instruction runs. The function object holds a reference to the module's globals dict (f.__globals__), not a snapshot of its values, so it sees whatever x is bound to at call time.

def f        →  f.__globals__ is the module dict
x = 20       →  module dict['x'] now 20
f()          →  LOAD_GLOBAL 'x' reads 20

Why the obvious guess fails. It's natural to picture def "capturing" the surroundings at the moment it runs, the way a photo would. Python does no capturing for globals at all, and even closures (see #53) capture variables, not values. Definition time only decides which scope a name comes from, not its value.

Try a variant. Delete the global and the same call fails at call time, not at definition time:

x = 10
def f():
    return x
del x
try:
    f()
except NameError as e:
    print(e)

name 'x' is not defined

In real code. Monkey-patching works because of this: tests replace module.helper and every function that calls helper picks up the fake on its next call. The flip side: a function that reads a module-level setting changes behaviour if any import rebinds that setting.

10. What's the output? 🟢 Low

print(type(1 / 2), 1 / 2, 4 / 2)
Answer

Output

<class 'float'> 0.5 2.0

In Python 3, / is true division and always returns a float, even when the result is a whole number (2.0). Use // for integer floor division.

11. What's the output? 🟢 Low

print(int("0b101", 0), int("ff", 16), int(3.99), int(-3.99))
Answer

Output

5 255 3 -3

int(s, 0) infers the base from the prefix (0b, 0o, 0x). int(float) truncates toward zero (-3.99 becomes -3), unlike // and math.floor, which round down (-4).

12. What's the output? 🔴 High · 🪤 Trap

a = b = []
a.append(1)
print(b)
a = a + [2]
print(a, b)
Answer

Output

[1]
[1, 2] [1]

a = b = [] makes one list with two names. append mutates that shared list. a + [2] builds a new list and rebinds a to it, so b still points at the old one.

Go deeper

Under the hood. a = b = [] evaluates the right side once and binds both names to the result, left to right. a.append(1) mutates the object in place. a = a + [2] calls list.__add__, which allocates a new list containing the old items plus 2, and then rebinds only a.

after a = b = []      a ─┬─▶ [ ]
                      b ─┘
after a.append(1)     a ─┬─▶ [1]
                      b ─┘
after a = a + [2]     a ───▶ [1, 2]   (new object)
                      b ───▶ [1]

Why the obvious guess fails. a = a + [2] and a += [2] look interchangeable, but they aren't for lists. + builds a new object, while += calls __iadd__ and mutates in place (see #25). With +=, b would have printed [1, 2] as well.

Try a variant. Swap + for += and the alias sees the change:

a = b = [1]
a += [2]
print(a, b, a is b)

[1, 2] [1, 2] True

In real code. Chained assignment with a mutable value (x = y = {}) is almost always a bug when you meant two separate containers. It's fine for immutables (i = j = 0), because you can never mutate an int in place, only rebind the name.

Strings (Q13–Q22)

13. What's the output? 🟡 Medium

s = "hello"
try:
    s[0] = "H"
except TypeError:
    print("TypeError")
print(s.replace("h", "H"), s)
Answer

Output

TypeError
Hello hello

Strings are immutable. Item assignment raises TypeError. Methods like replace return a new string and leave the original unchanged.

Go deeper

Under the hood. str has no item-assignment slot: its type doesn't implement sq_ass_item/__setitem__, so s[0] = "H" raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Every string method allocates and returns a new string. Immutability is what lets CPython cache a string's hash, intern it, and share it safely between threads and dict keys.

The edge cases. s += "x" looks like mutation but rebinds s to a new string. CPython sometimes optimises it to resize in place when the refcount is 1, which is why a loop of += isn't always quadratic, but that's an implementation detail you shouldn't depend on. "".join(parts) is the guaranteed linear way to build a string.

Try a variant. The original string object is untouched while the name moves on:

s = "hello"
before = id(s)
s = s.replace("h", "H")
print(s, id(s) == before)

Hello False

In real code. To change characters, convert and rebuild (list(s) → edit → "".join(...)), or use slicing ("H" + s[1:]). For many edits to a large text, collect the pieces in a list or use io.StringIO, then join once at the end.

14. What's the output? 🟢 Low

print("abc" * 2, "-".join("abc"), "a,b,,c".split(","))
Answer

Output

abcabc a-b-c ['a', 'b', '', 'c']

* repeats a sequence. join accepts any iterable of strings, and a string is an iterable of characters. split(",") keeps empty fields between consecutive delimiters.

15. What's the output? 🟢 Low · 🪤 Trap

print("  a b  c ".split())
print("  a b ".split(" "))
Answer

Output

['a', 'b', 'c']
['', '', 'a', 'b', '']

With no argument, split() splits on runs of whitespace and drops leading and trailing blanks. With an explicit separator, it splits on every single occurrence, which leaves empty strings behind.

Go deeper

Under the hood. str.split() with no argument (or sep=None) runs a different algorithm: it treats any run of whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines, Unicode spaces) as one separator and drops empty pieces at both ends. split(" ") treats the literal one-character string as the separator and returns a field for every occurrence, including the empty text between two adjacent spaces.

"  a b ".split(" ")
 ''│''│a│b│''        each │ is one space → 5 fields

Why the obvious guess fails. Both calls "split on spaces" in English, so people expect the same list. The no-argument form is really "split into words", the explicit form is "split on this exact delimiter", which is what you want for CSV-like data where empty fields are meaningful.

Try a variant. maxsplit and a mix of tabs and newlines:

print("a\tb\n c".split(), "k=v=w".split("=", 1))

['a', 'b', 'c'] ['k', 'v=w']

In real code. Parsing whitespace-separated input (log lines, ps output, competitive-programming input) → split(). Parsing a delimited format → split(","), or better the csv module, which also handles quoting. "".split() returns [] but "".split(",") returns [''], a frequent off-by-one in parsers.

16. What's the output? 🟡 Medium

s = "python"
print(s[::-1], s[1:4], s[-2:], repr(s[10:]))
Answer

Output

nohtyp yth on ''

The slice form is [start:stop:step], and stop is excluded. A negative step walks backward, so [::-1] reverses. Out-of-range slices never raise. They just return an empty string.

Go deeper

Under the hood. A slice s[start:stop:step] builds a slice object and calls slice.indices(len(s)), which clamps start and stop into range and fills in defaults that depend on the sign of step. With a negative step the defaults flip: start at the end, stop before the beginning. That's why [::-1] reverses without any special case.

 p  y  t  h  o  n
 0  1  2  3  4  5
-6 -5 -4 -3 -2 -1
s[1:4] → y t h      (stop 4 excluded)
s[-2:] → o n

The edge cases. Indexing (s[10]) raises IndexError, but slicing never does, it just returns '' when the clamped range is empty. A step of 0 is the one slice error: ValueError: slice step cannot be zero. Slices of strings, lists and tuples always copy.

Try a variant. indices() shows the clamped numbers Python actually uses:

s = "python"
print(slice(None, None, -1).indices(len(s)), slice(1, 100).indices(len(s)), s[::2])

(5, -1, -1) (1, 6, 1) pto

In real code. Slicing is the safe way to take "at most N": items[:10] never fails on short lists. Palindrome checks (s == s[::-1]) and "last N" (s[-n:]) are classic interview one-liners. Watch s[-0:], which is s[0:], the whole string, when n happens to be 0.

20. What's the output? 🟢 Low · 🪤 Trap

print("a" < "b", "Z" < "a", "apple" < "apricot", "10" < "9")
Answer

Output

True True True True

Strings compare lexicographically by code point. Uppercase letters (65–90) sort before lowercase (97–122). "10" < "9" because '1' < '9', so sort numeric strings with key=int.

Go deeper

Under the hood. str comparison walks both strings character by character and compares Unicode code points (ord(c)) at the first difference. If one string runs out first, the shorter one is smaller. There's no notion of numbers, words or locale.

Pair First difference Code points Result
"Z" < "a" Z vs a 90 < 97 True
"apple" < "apricot" p vs r 112 < 114 True
"10" < "9" 1 vs 9 49 < 57 True

Why the obvious guess fails. People expect "dictionary order" (case-insensitive) or numeric order for digit strings. Python gives neither: all uppercase letters sort before all lowercase, and "10" sorts before "9" because only the first character is compared.

Try a variant. Sorting version-like strings correctly needs a key:

v = ["10", "9", "100", "Apple", "apple"]
print(sorted(v), sorted(v[:3], key=int), sorted(v[3:], key=str.casefold))

['10', '100', '9', 'Apple', 'apple'] ['9', '10', '100'] ['Apple', 'apple']

In real code. File names like img10.png vs img9.png need a "natural sort" key that splits digits out. Human-facing names need str.casefold or locale.strxfrm. Never compare version strings as plain strings: use packaging.version.Version.

21. What's the output? 🟢 Low · 🪤 Trap

s = "banana"
print(s.count("an"), s.count("ana"), s.strip("ab"))
Answer

Output

2 1 nan

count finds non-overlapping matches, so "ana" counts once. strip("ab") treats its argument as a set of characters and strips them from both ends until it hits a character not in the set. It does not remove a prefix or suffix. Use removeprefix/removesuffix for that.

Go deeper

Under the hood. count(sub) scans left to right and, after each match, resumes after the match, so matches can't overlap. In "banana", "ana" matches at index 1, the scan jumps to index 4 ("na"), and there's no second match even though "ana" also starts at 3. strip(chars) treats chars as a set and removes any of those characters from both ends until it meets one outside the set.

strip("ab") on b a n a n a
               ↑ removed  ↑ removed (a), then n stops it
               → "nan"

Why the obvious guess fails. People read strip("ab") as "remove the prefix ab" and expect "nana", and they read count("ana") as "how many places does it appear", which is 2. Both methods were designed around different definitions than the English reading.

Try a variant. The prefix-removal method that does what people expect, and an overlapping count with a regex lookahead:

import re
s = "banana"
print(s.removeprefix("ba"), "xxaxx".strip("x"), len(re.findall("(?=ana)", s)))

nana a 2

In real code. url.strip("https://") is a classic bug: it eats leading h, t, p, s, : and / characters from the host too ("https://shop.com".strip("https://") gives "op.com"). Use removeprefix/removesuffix (3.9+) for fixed text.

run time:      "".join(["hel", "lo"]) → new "hello"          ◀── c

Answer

Output

dataclass refuses unhashable (mutable) defaults at class-creation time, which guards against the same shared-mutable-default bug as #49. Use field(default_factory=list) instead.

Go deeper

Under the hood. When @dataclass processes the class, it inspects each field's default. If the default's type is unhashable (list, dict, set, and since 3.11 any object whose class sets __hash__ = None), it raises ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field items is not allowed: use default_factory. That check is a heuristic for "this would be shared between instances", the bug in #49 and #101.

items: list = []   → default is a list (unhashable) → ValueError at class creation
items: list = field(default_factory=list) → generated __init__ calls list() per instance

The edge cases. The check uses hashability, not mutability. A mutable but hashable default (an instance of a plain user class) slips through and is shared. Tuples and frozensets are fine as defaults. Pydantic models accept items: list = [] because they copy the default per instance.

Try a variant. default_factory gives each instance its own list, while a hashable mutable object is still shared:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
class Bag:
    def __init__(self): self.items = []
@dataclass
class Cart:
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)
    bag: Bag = Bag()
a, b = Cart(), Cart()
a.items.append(1)
print(b.items, a.bag is b.bag)

[] True

In real code. Use field(default_factory=...) for lists, dicts, sets, and for any object you construct as a default (default_factory=Bag). The error is a deliberate guard rail that fires at import, which is much better than a shared-state bug found in production.
